procedural_history.impugned_order: Order made by the Industrial Tribunal granting the appellant permission to discharge the respondents under s. 33 of the Act.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Appeals Nos. 133 and 134 of 1952 were preferred to the Labour Appellate Tribunal of India at Madras by the employers challenging the findings made by the tribunal against them. The workmen also preferred an appeal, No. 168 of 1952, claiming a larger bonus. The employers then applied to the Appellate Tribunal for a review, which was dismissed. The Labour Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeals of the employers.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeal by special leave from the decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The appellants challenged the Labour Appellate Tribunal's decision refusing to review its decision. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal, and restored the order made by the Industrial Tribunal, Bihar.

directions: Set aside the decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal.
Restore the order made by the Industrial Tribunal, Bihar, on date May 14, 1953.
The appellant will be entitled to its costs of this appeal from the respondents.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Labour Appellate Tribunal has the jurisdiction to review its own orders under Order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

facts: The Labour Appellate Tribunal had dismissed a review application filed by the appellants.
The Tribunal's decision was based on two grounds: first, that it had no power to review its own orders, and second, that even if it did, no case for review had been made out.
law: The Supreme Court referenced its recent decision in M/s. Martin Burn Ltd. v. R. N. Banerjee.

In that case, it was established that the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) applies to proceedings before the Labour Appellate Tribunal, allowing it to exercise powers under provisions like Order 41 and Section 151 of the Code.
application: The Court reasoned that if the Code of Civil Procedure generally applies to the Tribunal's proceedings, then the provisions for review under Order 47 of the Code must also apply.
The Court noted that while the Martin Burn case did not specifically address Order 47, this did not matter.
The logic is that if other parts of the CPC apply, there is no reason to exclude the part concerning the power of review.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the Labour Appellate Tribunal erred in law by concluding that it had no jurisdiction to review its own order under the provisions of Order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

issue.issue_text: Whether an appeal lay from the decision of the Industrial Tribunal to the Labour Appellate Tribunal.

facts: An order was made by the Industrial Tribunal granting an appellant permission to discharge the respondents.
This decision was appealed to the Labour Appellate Tribunal, which interfered with the Industrial Tribunal's order.
law: The Supreme Court examined whether the Labour Appellate Tribunal had the legal authority, or jurisdiction, to hear an appeal from the decision of the Industrial Tribunal in this matter.
application: The Court determined that, in this case, the law did not provide for an appeal from the Industrial Tribunal's decision to the Labour Appellate Tribunal.
Because no appeal was legally permissible, the Court found that the Labour Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order made by the Industrial Tribunal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that no appeal lay from the decision of the Industrial Tribunal to the Labour Appellate Tribunal. Consequently, the Labour Appellate Tribunal's decision was set aside, and the original order of the Industrial Tribunal was restored.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Labour Appellate Tribunal has the jurisdiction to review its own orders under Order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
appellant_arguments: The Labour Appellate Tribunal was in error in holding that it had no jurisdiction to review its decision under Order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The Tribunal has the power to correct a mistake apparent on the face of the record under its powers of review.
respondent_arguments: The Labour Appellate Tribunal correctly held that it had no power of review.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an appeal lay from the decision of the Industrial Tribunal to the Labour Appellate Tribunal.
appellant_arguments: An appeal was maintainable from the Industrial Tribunal to the Labour Appellate Tribunal, as demonstrated by their action of filing such an appeal.
respondent_arguments: No appeal lay from the decision of the Industrial Tribunal to the Labour Appellate Tribunal. (This point was raised for the first time before the Supreme Court).

cases.case_name: Mis. Martin Burn Ltd. v. R. N. Banerjee
cases.principle: The Code of Civil Procedure applies to proceedings before the Labour Appellate Tribunal, with the result that the appellate tribunal can exercise its powers under Order 41, Rule 21 as well as under Section 151 of the Code.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Code of Civil Procedure applies to proceedings before the Labour Appellate Tribunal; consequently, the tribunal has the jurisdiction to review its own orders under the provisions of Order 47 of the Code.
obiter: The court may choose to deal with the merits of an argument that was not orally urged at the proper stage if a written statement had been filed expressly and specifically raising the point.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Labour Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to hear the appeal from the Industrial Tribunal's decision. Because the Appellate Tribunal acted without jurisdiction, its decision is void and must be set aside, restoring the original order of the Industrial Tribunal.
legal_tests_applied: If the Code of Civil Procedure applies generally to proceedings before the Labour Appellate Tribunal, then its specific provisions, such as Order 47 (review), also apply to those proceedings unless explicitly excluded.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant lost on the key jurisdictional issue of whether an appeal was maintainable from the Industrial Tribunal to the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The Supreme Court concluded that no such appeal lay, which rendered the entire proceeding before the Labour Appellate Tribunal invalid.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that no appeal lay from the decision of the Industrial Tribunal to the Labour Appellate Tribunal. This argument, though raised for the first time before the Supreme Court, was accepted as a fatal jurisdictional flaw in the proceedings below, leading to the nullification of the Appellate Tribunal's order.
policy_considerations: The court will entertain a critical jurisdictional argument even if raised for the first time on final appeal, based on the principle that a party should not be deprived of the benefit of any argument which could possibly be advanced in their favour.
